title: The examen
hookLine: Ignatius's daily look back: thanks, light, review, sorrow, hope

lines: ONLY TWO BOOKS IN THE HOUSE.
cards: In 1521, a young Basque soldier named Iñigo was defending the fortress of Pamplona when a cannonball smashed his leg. Months in bed, bored out of his mind, he asked for adventure novels.
The house only had a life of Christ and a book of saints. He read them, and noticed something odd: daydreams of glory left him empty afterward, and daydreams of following Christ left him glad.
He'd started paying attention to what was happening inside him. That soldier became Saint Ignatius of Loyola, and the habit became today's word.

teach.h: EXAMEN: THE NEEDLE ON A SCALE.
teach.b: First, the word. Examen is Latin, with a lovely old meaning: the needle on a balance scale, the little pointer that shows which way things tip. An examen is a daily look at which way your day tipped.
Second, the steps. In his Spiritual Exercises, published in 1548, Ignatius lays out a short daily prayer in five points, often summed up today in five words.
Thanks: remember what you were given today. Light: ask God for the grace to see your day clearly and honestly. Review: walk back through it hour by hour, like watching a film.
Where was there life? Where did you go wrong? Sorrow: ask forgiveness for what needs it.
Hope: look toward tomorrow, and ask for help with it. Third, the order.

What comes first isn't your sins. It's thanks. Ignatius puts gratitude before examining anything, and many who teach the examen say that's the secret: you look at your day as someone who has been loved all day long.
It's not an audit. It's a conversation about the day with someone who was there. Fourth, why it lasts.
Ignatius founded the Jesuits, and the story is often told that he let his companions shorten other prayers when they were busy or sick, but never the examen.
Today it's prayed in Jesuit schools, in homes at bedtime, even by people who've never met a Jesuit.
It takes ten or fifteen minutes, and at its heart is your line: where was God today?

how: Many Catholics, especially those formed by the Jesuits, pray the examen once or twice a day, often at night, and an examination of conscience is also how Catholics prepare for confession.

games.q: you're Iñigo, laid up for months with a shattered leg. you ask for adventure novels. what does the house have?
o: only a life of Christ and a book of saints.
games.why: he read them, noticed which daydreams left him empty and which left him glad, and started paying attention inside. the examen grew from that.

practice: Walk the five steps through today so far: name one thing you're grateful for, ask to see honestly, then run back through the day like a film on fast forward, stopping where you felt most alive and where you felt worst.
Name anything that needs forgiving, then think of the rest of today. If you pray, do all five with God; if you don't, do them with honest attention.

wordCard.voice: Examen. Latin for the needle on a scale: Saint Ignatius's daily five-step look back at the day, beginning with thanks. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the needle or tongue of a balance scale; also a testing, an examination.

carryVoice: Your line: where was god today. One moment is enough of an answer. Two hundred thirty-seven days in.

sources.ref: Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, no. 43 (the general examen)
